headline: Proves a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial depends only on the shape of its Bruhat interval, settling combinatorial invariance.
scope: Equal-parameter Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials for Bruhat intervals in every Coxeter system, finite or infinite, including comparisons across different systems.
plain: Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are attached to pairs of elements in symmetry groups and carry deep geometric information. Each pair also has a Bruhat interval, the set of elements between them, ordered like a family tree. The combinatorial invariance conjecture says the polynomial can be read from the bare shape of that ordered set. The paper proves this for all Coxeter groups, and a computer proof checker has a formal version.
doesNot: This does not give a simple recipe for computing the polynomial from the interval's shape. It also covers only the equal-parameter polynomials, not unequal-parameter versions.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Matthew Dyer, published formulation of the conjecture attributed to Lusztig and Dyer
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the full combinatorial invariance conjecture of Lusztig and Dyer, earlier known only in special cases, with a Lean statement.

explanation:
Take the 24 orderings of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, which form the symmetric group S4. Each ordering has a length: the number of pairs that appear in the wrong order. Bruhat order says when one ordering sits below another, roughly by fixing wrong pairs one at a time. Now pick 3412, which has length 4. The orderings between 1234 and 3412 form its Bruhat interval. A computer count finds 14 orderings in it. Kazhdan and Lusztig attached a polynomial to each such pair. For this pair it is 1 + q. For the whole group, from 1234 to 4321, the interval has 24 orderings and the polynomial is 1. We computed these values with the standard recursion.

Kazhdan and Lusztig defined these polynomials through an algebra built from the group[1]. Later they found a geometric meaning, as local invariants of certain spaces called Schubert varieties[2]. The interval, by contrast, is just a finite ordered set. The combinatorial invariance conjecture is attributed to Lusztig and Dyer[3]. It says two intervals with the same order shape have the same polynomial. Before this paper, it was known for intervals starting at the identity, in every Coxeter group[4]. It was also known for all intervals of rank at most six[5]. Here rank is the difference in length between the two ends.

The paper proves the full conjecture. For any two Coxeter systems, an order-preserving match between two intervals forces equal polynomials[6]. A Coxeter system is a group generated by reflections, like S4 or the symmetries of a regular polygon. The result covers infinite and noncrystallographic groups too[7]. The obstacle is that a bare interval keeps no labels: no generators and no root data[8]. The proof works with sheaves on moment graphs, which recover the polynomial as a rank. It orders the edges of one interval using a reflection order from the other system[9]. A two-way comparison then forces every bound in the argument to be exact[10].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the main theorem. It covers intervals from two different Coxeter systems. So the paper proves it, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. No specialist review of the paper is published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if it holds up: it settles a long-standing named conjecture in full generality, and Lean has a formal statement of the main theorem. No specialist review is published.
